questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: What is the function of the chordae tendineae?
questions.modelAnswer:
- The atria are thin-walled receiving chambers, whereas the ventricles are thicker pumping chambers; the left ventricular wall is substantially thicker than the right.
- The right atrium contains the sinus venarum, crista terminalis, pectinate muscles, and fossa ovalis; ventricular interiors contain trabeculae carneae, papillary muscles, and atrioventricular valves.
- Chordae tendineae tether valve cusps to papillary muscles and prevent prolapse during systole without actively opening the valves.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.topic: Microscopic Structure of Cardiac Muscle Fibers
questions.text: Compare the junctions found in the transverse versus the longitudinal portions of the intercalated disc.
questions.modelAnswer:
Transverse portion (crosses the fiber at right angles, at the level of the Z line): contains gap junctions, fascia adherens, and macula adherens (desmosomes).
Longitudinal portion (runs parallel to the long axis of the fiber): contains gap junctions only, and these are the predominant site of electrical coupling between cells.
questions.explanation: The transverse portion bears the adhering junctions (fascia adherens, desmosomes) that transmit contractile force between cells, while the longitudinal portion is dominated by gap junctions that electrically couple adjacent cardiomyocytes for synchronized contraction.
questions.keyConcept: Transverse discs favor mechanical adhesion; longitudinal discs favor electrical (gap-junction) coupling.

questions.subject: Histology

questions.text: Describe the ultrastructural features of thick myofilaments (myosin) in the dark A band.
questions.modelAnswer: Thick myofilaments run parallel to one another in the A band. Their central portions are linked transversely at the M line within the H zone, while their projecting myosin heads form cross-bridges toward surrounding thin filaments.
questions.explanation: A complete answer should identify the relevant microscopic structures and connect each structural feature to its function in cardiac muscle, blood vessels, capillaries, or lymphatics.
questions.keyConcept: Accurate cardiovascular histology depends on relating microscopic organization to mechanical, conductive, exchange, or drainage function.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.topic: Microscopic Structure of Cardiac Muscle Fibers
questions.text: Enumerate the organelles involved in the contractile process of cardiac muscle fibers.
questions.modelAnswer:
a. Myofibrils (the contractile elements: actin and myosin filaments organized into sarcomeres).
b. T-tubules (transmit the wave of depolarization from the sarcolemma into the cell interior).
c. Sarcoplasmic reticulum — sarcotubules and terminal cisternae (store and release calcium for excitation-contraction coupling).
d. Mitochondria (supply the large amount of ATP needed for continuous, fatigue-resistant contraction).
questions.explanation: Cardiac contraction depends on coordinated organelles: myofibrils generate force, T-tubules propagate the electrical signal inward, the sarcoplasmic reticulum handles calcium flux, and abundant mitochondria meet the high, continuous energy demand of the myocardium.
questions.keyConcept: Contraction requires coordinated myofibrils, T-tubules, sarcoplasmic reticulum, and mitochondria.

questions.text: What are cardiac T-tubules?

questions.explanation: As a subendocardial structure carrying Purkinje (conduction) fibers, the moderator band is identified within the subendocardial connective tissue.
questions.keyConcept: Moderator band lies within the subendocardium.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.topic: Microscopic Structure of Cardiac Muscle Fibers
questions.text: Light microscopic structure of the cardiac muscle fibers is characterized by:
questions.explanation: Unlike skeletal muscle, cardiac fibers lack satellite cells entirely; they are branched, surrounded by a basement membrane, and have a single central (not peripheral, flattened) nucleus.
questions.keyConcept: Absence of satellite cells underlies the very limited regenerative capacity of cardiac muscle.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.topic: Microscopic Structure of Cardiac Muscle Fibers
questions.text: Longitudinal portion of intercalated disc differs from the transverse portion in which of the following?
options: It is parallel to the long axis of the fibers.
It is crossing the fibers at right angle.
It contains few and small gap junctions.
questions.explanation: The longitudinal (lateral, step) portions of the intercalated disc run parallel to the long axis of the fiber and are rich in gap junctions, whereas the transverse portions cross the fiber at right angles and are rich in fascia adherens and desmosomes.
questions.keyConcept: Longitudinal portions run parallel to the fiber and carry most gap junctions; transverse portions cross at right angles and carry adherens junctions/desmosomes.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.topic: Microscopic Structure of Cardiac Muscle Fibers
questions.text: Moderator band is composed of which of the following?
questions.explanation: Purkinje fibers, which make up the moderator band, are modified (specialized) cardiac muscle fibers adapted for fast conduction rather than for contraction.
questions.keyConcept: Purkinje fibers = modified cardiomyocytes specialized for conduction.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.topic: Microscopic Structure of Cardiac Muscle Fibers
questions.text: Purkinje fibers are present at which of the following layers?
questions.explanation: Purkinje fibers, the terminal fibers of the cardiac conduction system, lie within the subendocardial connective tissue layer.
questions.keyConcept: Purkinje fibers are located in the subendocardium.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.topic: Microscopic Structure of Cardiac Muscle Fibers
questions.text: Purkinje fibers differ from cardiac muscle fiber in which of the following?
options: Scattered among the cardiac muscle fibers.
questions.explanation: Purkinje fibers are specialized for rapid impulse conduction rather than forceful contraction, so they contain far fewer myofibrils (and abundant glycogen) compared with ordinary contractile cardiomyocytes, which they are also larger than and paler-staining, not smaller or deeply stained.
questions.keyConcept: Purkinje fibers: few myofibrils, high glycogen, built for conduction not contraction.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.topic: Microscopic Structure of Cardiac Muscle Fibers
questions.text: Regeneration of cardiac muscle fibers is characterized by which of the following?
options: Don't increase in size or length.
questions.explanation: Because cardiac muscle essentially cannot regenerate, damaged myocardium is repaired by fibrous (scar) tissue rather than by new muscle fiber formation.
questions.keyConcept: Cardiac injury heals by fibrosis, not true regeneration.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.topic: Microscopic Structure of Cardiac Muscle Fibers
questions.text: The outer layer of epicardium is lined by which type of epithelium?
questions.explanation: The outer surface of the epicardium (visceral layer of the serous pericardium) is covered by mesothelium, a simple squamous epithelium of serosal origin.
questions.keyConcept: Epicardium's outer covering is mesothelium.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.topic: Microscopic Structure of Cardiac Muscle Fibers
questions.text: The structural and functional unit of the cardiac muscle fibers is called:
questions.explanation: The sarcomere, the segment between two successive Z lines containing an organized set of actin and myosin filaments, is the basic contractile unit of all striated muscle including cardiac muscle.
questions.keyConcept: Sarcomere = basic contractile unit of striated muscle.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.topic: Microscopic Structure of Cardiac Muscle Fibers
questions.text: The T-tubules of the cardiac muscle fibers differ from that of the skeletal muscle fibers in which of the following:
questions.explanation: Cardiac T-tubules pair with only one terminal cisterna of the sarcoplasmic reticulum to form a diad, whereas skeletal muscle T-tubules are flanked by two terminal cisternae, forming a triad at the A-I junction.
questions.keyConcept: Cardiac muscle = diad; skeletal muscle = triad.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.topic: Microscopic Structure of Cardiac Muscle Fibers
questions.text: Which of the following about Z line is true?
options: Actin myofilaments are attached to it.
questions.explanation: The Z line/disc is the site of attachment for the thin (actin) myofilaments of two adjoining sarcomeres, and it defines the sarcomere boundary rather than being located within the A band or bisected by the M line.
questions.keyConcept: Z line anchors actin filaments and marks sarcomere boundaries.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.topic: Microscopic Structure of Cardiac Muscle Fibers
questions.text: Which of the following characterize the cardiac muscle fibers?
questions.explanation: Cardiac muscle shows cross-striations from its organized sarcomeric myofilaments, but unlike skeletal muscle it contracts involuntarily under autonomic/pacemaker control rather than conscious control.
questions.keyConcept: Cardiac muscle is striated yet involuntary.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.topic: Microscopic Structure of Cardiac Muscle Fibers
questions.text: Which of the following defines the T-tubule?
options: Finger like projection of the sarcolemma at the A-I junction.
Invagination of the sarcolemma at the level of Z line.
Structural and functional unit of cardiac muscle fibers.
The site at which two adjacent cardiac cells are joined.
questions.explanation: Cardiac T-tubules are deep tubular invaginations of the sarcolemma located at the Z line (unlike skeletal muscle, where they invaginate at the A-I junction), allowing the action potential to reach the cell interior rapidly.
questions.keyConcept: Cardiac T-tubules invaginate the sarcolemma at the Z line.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.topic: Microscopic Structure of Cardiac Muscle Fibers
questions.text: Which of the following is correct about the cardiac muscle diad?
options: Formed of two cisternae of sarcoplasmic reticulum.
Formed of two cisternae of sarcoplasmic reticulum and rER.
questions.explanation: The cardiac diad, composed of one T-tubule apposed to one terminal cisterna of the sarcoplasmic reticulum, is located at the Z line, matching the position of cardiac T-tubules.
questions.keyConcept: Cardiac diad is located at the Z line.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.topic: Microscopic Structure of Cardiac Muscle Fibers
questions.text: Which of the following is NOT present in the cytoplasm of the cardiac muscle fibers?
questions.explanation: Cardiac myocyte cytoplasm normally contains glycogen granules, smooth ER (sarcoplasmic reticulum), abundant mitochondria, and age-related lipofuscin pigment, but melanin pigment is not a normal constituent of cardiac muscle.
questions.keyConcept: Lipofuscin (not melanin) accumulates with age in cardiomyocytes.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.topic: Microscopic Structure of Cardiac Muscle Fibers
questions.text: Which of the following is NOT seen in L/M examination of cardiac valves?
questions.explanation: Cardiac valve leaflets are avascular, largely acellular dense connective tissue (rich in collagen and elastic fibers) covered by an endothelium of simple squamous cells; they do not contain cardiac muscle fibers.
questions.keyConcept: Valve leaflets = connective tissue + endothelium, with no muscle fibers.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.topic: Microscopic Structure of Cardiac Muscle Fibers
questions.text: Which of the following is the moderator band?
options: Left branch of AV bundle of His
Right branch of AV bundle of His.
questions.explanation: The moderator band is a muscular trabecula carrying the right bundle branch of the AV (His) bundle directly to the anterior papillary muscle of the right ventricle.
questions.keyConcept: Moderator band carries the right bundle branch of the AV bundle.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.topic: Microscopic Structure of Cardiac Muscle Fibers
questions.text: Which of the following junctions is responsible for the function of cardiac muscle fibers in coordinated form through direct communication between cells?
questions.explanation: Gap junctions form low-resistance channels that allow ions and action potentials to pass directly from one cardiomyocyte to the next, coordinating synchronous contraction of the myocardium.
questions.keyConcept: Gap junctions provide electrical coupling between cardiomyocytes.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.topic: Microscopic Structure of Cardiac Muscle Fibers
questions.text: Which of the following junctions prevents separation of the muscle cells during contraction?
questions.explanation: Desmosomes (macula adherens) anchor intermediate (desmin) filaments between adjoining cardiomyocytes, supplying the mechanical strength that keeps cells from pulling apart during contraction.
questions.keyConcept: Desmosomes provide mechanical adhesion at the intercalated disc.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.topic: Microscopic Structure of Cardiac Muscle Fibers
questions.text: Which of the following organoids characterize the cardiac muscle fibers?
questions.explanation: Although several organelles occur in cardiomyocytes, the sarcoplasmic reticulum is the organelle most specifically associated with cardiac muscle because it stores and releases the Ca2+ needed for excitation-contraction coupling, making it the most characteristic choice among the options.
questions.keyConcept: Sarcoplasmic reticulum stores/releases Ca2+ for contraction.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.topic: Microscopic Structure of Cardiac Muscle Fibers
questions.text: Which of the following structures in the cardiac muscle fibers has a role in controlling blood pressure?
questions.explanation: Atrial cardiomyocytes secrete atrial natriuretic factor (ANF/ANP), a hormone that promotes natriuresis, diuresis, and vasodilation, helping regulate blood volume and pressure.
questions.keyConcept: ANF/ANP, secreted by atrial myocytes, lowers blood pressure.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.topic: Microscopic Structure of Cardiac Muscle Fibers
questions.text: Which type of connective tissue forms the cardiac skeleton?
questions.explanation: The fibrous cardiac skeleton (annuli fibrosi and valve rings) is built of dense irregular connective tissue, giving it the strength to anchor the valves and electrically insulate atria from ventricles.
questions.keyConcept: Cardiac skeleton = dense irregular connective tissue.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Define cardiac reserve and describe its long-lasting mechanisms.
questions.modelAnswer:
- Cardiac output equals heart rate multiplied by stroke volume; stroke volume equals end-diastolic volume minus end-systolic volume.
- Preload and venous return increase output through Frank-Starling heterometric regulation, while contractility supports homeometric regulation and lowers end-systolic volume.
- Sympathetic stimulation raises heart rate and contractility, whereas excessive tachycardia can reduce filling and output.
- Cardiac reserve is the difference between maximal and resting output and is recruited by increased rate, preload, contractility, and longer-term hypertrophy when appropriate.
questions.explanation: Cardiac reserve is the difference between the maximal cardiac output achievable and the resting cardiac output; intrinsic mechanisms (Frank-Starling, hypertrophy) can raise output roughly two-fold on their own, while further increases toward maximal exertion require sympathoadrenal activation. Use this principle to structure a complete answer to: “Define cardiac reserve and describe its long-lasting mechanisms.”
questions.keyConcept: Cardiac reserve = maximal minus basal output; intrinsic vs. sympathetic limits

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: List the 3 mechanisms of sympathetic stimulation to increase the heart rate.
questions.modelAnswer:
- First: increases inward Na+ current (If) to increase the rate of diastolic (pacemaker) depolarization.
- Second: increased intracellular cAMP facilitates the opening of L-type Ca2+ channels, increasing Ca2+ influx and producing a more rapid upstroke of the action potential.
- Third: inactivates K+ channels, thus decreasing outward K+ current, so the threshold for firing is reached more quickly.
questions.explanation: Cardiac electrical activity arises from time- and voltage-dependent ion-channel currents that generate distinct action-potential shapes in nodal versus contractile tissue; the plateau (phase 2) of ventricular myocytes reflects a balance of inward calcium and outward potassium currents that prolongs the refractory period. questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: List the 3 mechanisms of vagal stimulation to decrease the heart rate.
questions.modelAnswer:
- First: decreases inward Na+ current (If) to decrease the rate of diastolic (pacemaker) depolarization.
- Second: decreased intracellular cAMP slows the opening of Ca2+ channels, resulting in a decrease in the firing rate of the action potential.
- Third: opens a special set of K+ channels (IK,ACh), resulting in an enhanced outward K+ current, which leads to a decreased rate of diastolic depolarization (hyperpolarization).

questions.text: What is the mechanism of pacemaker potential?
questions.modelAnswer:
- The first inward current is carried mainly by Na+ and conducted through funny (If) channels.
- The second current is an inward Ca2+ current, due to opening of the T (transient)-type Ca2+ channels.
- There is a progressive decline in outward K+ current during phase 4; if this decline did not occur, it would compensate for the continuous slow influx of Na+ in the first part of the pacemaker potential and the slow influx of Ca2+ in the later part, and threshold would not be reached.
- Together, the falling K+ efflux and rising Na+/Ca2+ influx drive the membrane potential toward threshold, at which point the L-type Ca2+ channels open to generate the upstroke of the action potential.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Define heart failure. List its causes.
questions.modelAnswer:
- Heart failure is the inability of the heart to provide adequate output at normal filling pressures or only by using elevated filling pressures.
- Systolic failure impairs ejection and lowers ejection fraction; diastolic failure impairs relaxation or compliance with relatively preserved ejection fraction.
- Left-sided failure causes pulmonary congestion and dyspnea, while right-sided failure causes systemic venous congestion, edema, hepatomegaly, and raised jugular venous pressure.
- Neurohumoral compensation initially supports pressure and perfusion but promotes fluid retention and remodeling.
questions.explanation: In heart failure, reduced contractility or increased afterload/preload shifts the ventricular function (Frank-Starling) curve downward and to the right; compensatory neurohormonal activation (sympathetic and renin-angiotensin-aldosterone) initially supports output but eventually worsens remodeling and symptoms. questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Compare the in parallel arrangement with the in series arrangement.
questions.modelAnswer:
- The cardiovascular system maintains tissue perfusion and homeostasis by transporting gases, nutrients, hormones, heat, and waste.
- Elastic arteries buffer pulsatile ejection, muscular arteries distribute flow, arterioles provide the major adjustable resistance, capillaries provide exchange, and veins serve as high-capacitance reservoirs.
- Pressure falls most across arterioles, velocity is lowest in capillaries because their total cross-sectional area is greatest, and venous capacitance is highest.
- Parallel organ circuits permit independent flow regulation and lower total resistance.
questions.explanation: The cardiovascular system is a closed circuit in which the heart generates pressure to drive blood through the pulmonary and systemic circulations in series, delivering oxygen and nutrients and removing metabolic waste, while also serving endocrine, thermoregulatory, and immune-transport roles. questions.text: Compare between the different types of cardiac muscles.
questions.modelAnswer:
- The fibrous cardiac skeleton supports valve annuli and electrically insulates atria from ventricles except through the AV bundle.
- Intercalated discs contain desmosomes and fascia adherens for mechanical linkage and gap junctions for electrical coupling, creating a functional syncytium.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Describe the characters that make the SA node acts as the natural pacemaker of the heart.
questions.modelAnswer:
- Fast-response myocardial action potentials have phases 0–4: rapid sodium-mediated depolarization, brief early repolarization, a calcium-potassium plateau, potassium-mediated repolarization, and a stable resting potential.
- SA and AV nodal slow-response cells lack a stable resting potential; funny current and calcium currents produce phase-4 depolarization, L-type calcium channels generate phase 0, and potassium efflux produces phase 3.
- Sympathetic stimulation steepens phase 4 and accelerates firing, whereas vagal stimulation hyperpolarizes nodal cells and flattens phase 4.
- The prolonged refractory period prevents tetanus and supports coordinated pumping.

questions.modelAnswer:
- A standard 12-lead ECG records cardiac electrical activity using three bipolar limb leads, three augmented limb leads, and six precordial leads.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Discuss re-entry phenomenon.
questions.modelAnswer:
- Cardiac arrhythmias arise from abnormal automaticity, triggered activity, or re-entry, and from conduction block.
- Re-entry requires a circuit, unidirectional block, and conduction slow enough for previously refractory tissue to recover.
- Early afterdepolarizations occur during prolonged repolarization, whereas delayed afterdepolarizations follow repolarization and are promoted by intracellular calcium overload.
- ECG classification uses rate, regularity, P-wave activity, PR conduction, and QRS width; heart block is graded by PR prolongation, dropped beats, or complete atrioventricular dissociation.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Compare between the absolute and the relative refractory periods in fast response and slow response action potentials.
questions.modelAnswer:
- Fast-response myocardial action potentials have phases 0–4: rapid sodium-mediated depolarization, brief early repolarization, a calcium-potassium plateau, potassium-mediated repolarization, and a stable resting potential.
- SA and AV nodal slow-response cells lack a stable resting potential; funny current and calcium currents produce phase-4 depolarization, L-type calcium channels generate phase 0, and potassium efflux produces phase 3.
- Sympathetic stimulation steepens phase 4 and accelerates firing, whereas vagal stimulation hyperpolarizes nodal cells and flattens phase 4.
- The prolonged refractory period prevents tetanus and supports coordinated pumping.
questions.explanation: Cardiac excitability depends on the resting membrane potential and sodium-channel availability; the long absolute refractory period of ventricular myocytes, driven by the calcium-dependent plateau, prevents tetanic contraction and limits re-entrant arrhythmias by ensuring the muscle cannot be re-excited until it has substantially relaxed. questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: A 75-year-old man goes to the hospital emergency department in coma. One minute later he is alert. An ECG shows 75 P waves per minute and 35 QRS waves per minute with a normal QRS shape and duration. Which of the following is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The ECG description (P rate 75, QRS rate 35, dissociation) indicates Third- Degree Heart Block. The clinical presentation of sudden syncope (coma) followed by alertness due to intermittent cessation of cardiac output in the setting of heart block is classically termed Stokes- Adams Syndrome. a) First-degree A-V block - FALSE because First-degree block is asymptomatic and has a 1:1 P: QRS ratio. c) Atrial paroxysmal tachycardia - FALSE because Paroxysmal tachycardias (SVT) typically cause palpitations or dizziness, rarely profound coma, and would show rapid rates (>150 bpm). d) Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia - FALSE because Paroxysmal tachycardias (SVT) typically cause palpitations or dizziness, rarely profound coma, and would show rapid rates (>150 bpm). e) Atrial premature contractions - FALSE because APCs are benign irregularities.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Hyperkalaemia may produce which effect on T waves?
questions.explanation: Hyperkalemia (high K+) increases potassium conductance (gK), accelerating Phase 3 repolarization. This creates a distinctive narrow-based, tall, “tented” T wave. It is the earliest ECG sign of hyperkalemia. a) Normal T wave - FALSE because Normal T waves are broad and asymmetrical. c) Low voltage - FALSE because Low voltage and inversion are associated with Hypokalemia or Ischemia. d) Inverted T wave - FALSE because Low voltage and inversion are associated with Hypokalemia or Ischemia.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: If there is a blockage between the AV node and the AV bundle, how will this affect the appearance of the ECG?
options: There would be more P waves than QRS complexes
There would be more QRS complexes than P waves
The T wave would be absent
questions.explanation: If a block exists between the AV node and bundle (Second or Third Degree), the atria continue to fire at the sinus rate, but fewer impulses reach the ventricles. Thus, the number of atrial depolarizations (P) exceeds ventricular depolarizations (QRS). a) PR interval would be smaller - FALSE because A block would prolong or dissociate the interval, not shorten it. b) QRS interval would be shorter - FALSE because QRS duration depends on the site of the ventricular escape rhythm. d) There would be more QRS complexes than P waves - FALSE because “More QRS than P” occurs in Ventricular Tachycardia or Junctional Tachycardia, not AV block. e) The T wave would be absent - FALSE because The T wave is unrelated to the site of the block.

Because the vector moves away from the positive poles of inferior leads (II, Ill, aVF), the P wave is inverted b) Atrial fibrillation - FALSE because Atrial Fibrillation exhibits chaotic “f” waves, not distinct P waves. c) Vagal stimulation - FALSE because Vagal stimulation causes sinus bradycardia but does not typically invert the P-wave axis. d) Heart block - FALSE because Heart block affects conduction time (PR), not the P-wave morphology.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: The diagnosis of a first-degree heart block is made in which of the following cases?
options: Asynchrony of P waves & QRS complexes
Fixed, prolonged PR interval followed by a nonconducted QRS complex at regular intervals
Normal PR interval, normal QRS complexes, increased R-R interval
Prolonged PR interval with every P wave followed by a QRS complex
The PR interval is progressively prolonged6. A until a QRS complex is dropped
questions.explanation: First-Degree AV Block is defined physiologically as a conduction delay (usually within the AV Node) where every atrial impulse still successfully reaches the ventricles (1:1 ratio), but the transit time is prolonged (PR>0.20 sec). a) Asynchrony of P waves and QRS complexes - FALSE because Asynchrony describes Third- Degree (Complete) Block (AV Dissociation). b) Fixed, prolonged PR interval followed by a nonconducted QRS complex at regular intervals - FALSE because Fixed PR with dropped beats describes Second-Degree Mobitz Type II. c) Normal PR interval, normal QRS complexes, increased R-R interval - FALSE because This describes Sinus Bradycardia, not a heart block. e) The PR interval is progressively prolonged until a QRS complex is dropped - FALSE because Progressive prolongation describes Second-Degree Mobitz Type I (Wenckebach).

questions.subject: Physiology

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Compare between the different heart sounds.
questions.modelAnswer:
- The cardiac cycle consists of atrial systole, isovolumetric ventricular contraction, rapid and reduced ejection, isovolumetric relaxation, rapid filling, and reduced filling.
- AV valves close at the start of ventricular systole to produce S1; semilunar valves close at the start of diastole to produce S2.
- Ventricular volume is constant during both isovolumetric phases, decreases during ejection, and increases during filling.
- The pressure-volume loop summarizes filling, isovolumetric contraction, ejection, and isovolumetric relaxation; its width is stroke volume and its area is stroke work.

questions.chapterTitle: Contractile Activity of the Cardiac Muscle
questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Describe the excitation-contraction coupling of cardiac muscles.
questions.modelAnswer:
- Cardiac contraction begins when L-type calcium entry during the action potential triggers calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum.
- Calcium binds troponin C, permits actin-myosin cycling, and is then removed by SERCA, the sodium-calcium exchanger, and sarcolemmal calcium pumps.
- Increased preload raises force through the Frank-Starling mechanism, whereas increased afterload reduces shortening and stroke volume.
- Increased contractility raises calcium availability, stroke volume, and ejection fraction while lowering end-systolic volume.

questions.chapterTitle: Contractile Activity of the Cardiac Muscle
questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Describe the methods of gradation of cardiac muscle contractions.
questions.modelAnswer:
- The fibrous cardiac skeleton supports valve annuli and electrically insulates atria from ventricles except through the AV bundle.
- Intercalated discs contain desmosomes and fascia adherens for mechanical linkage and gap junctions for electrical coupling, creating a functional syncytium.
- Papillary muscles tense chordae tendineae during systole to prevent AV-valve prolapse.
- Cardiac T tubules and sarcoplasmic reticulum coordinate calcium entry and calcium-induced calcium release for contraction.

questions.explanation: Water Hammer Pulse (Collapsing Pulse) is caused by a wide pulse pressure (high systolic, low diastolic). Causes include Aortic Regurgitation (volume runoff), Hyperthyroidism (hyperdynamic), and Arteriosclerosis (stiff vessels/high systolic). a) Arteriosclerosis - FALSE because Valid. Stiff arteries cause very high systolic pressure but lose elastic recoil (low diastolic pressure), creating a wide pulse pressure. b) Hyperthyroidism - FALSE because Valid. High metabolic rate causes peripheral vasodilation (low diastolic) and increased contractility (high systolic). c) Aortic regurgitation - FALSE because Valid. The classic cause. Blood leaks back into LV (very low diastolic) and LV pumps extra volume (high systolic). e) None of the above - FALSE because Incorrect because all three conditions listed can cause a wide pulse pressure.

questions.text: Compare between the heterometric and the homeometric intrinsic regulation of the cardiac output.
questions.modelAnswer:

- Cardiac reserve is the difference between maximal and resting output and is recruited by increased rate, preload, contractility, and longer-term hypertrophy when appropriate.

questions.text: Compare between Heterometric regulation & Homeometric regulation.
questions.modelAnswer:
| Feature | Heterometric regulation (Frank-Starling mechanism) | Homeometric regulation (e.g., Anrep effect, Bowditch effect) |
|---|---|---|
| Definition | Depends on a change in EDV (preload); an increased ventricular end-diastolic volume increases stroke volume/CO | Operates at the same EDV; contractility changes without a change in fiber length |
| Stimulus | Changes in venous return (preload) | A rise in afterload (Anrep effect) or heart rate (Bowditch effect) |
| Type | Preload phenomenon | Afterload/rate phenomenon |
| Time course | Prolonged and not time-limited | Transient, lasting only seconds up to 2 to 5 minutes |
| Clinical relevance | Important in postural changes, exercise-induced increases in CO, and in denervated/transplanted hearts; the failing heart depends more on this mechanism | Becomes important in conditions of increased afterload such as hypertension and aortic stenosis |
questions.explanation: Cardiac contraction follows excitation-contraction coupling, in which calcium influx through L-type channels triggers calcium-induced calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum; contractile strength is then graded by preload (Frank-Starling), afterload, and contractility (inotropy). questions.text: Draw the length tension relationship.
questions.modelAnswer:
A cardiac length-tension diagram plots developed (active) tension and diastolic (passive) tension against sarcomere length or end-diastolic ventricular volume on the x-axis:
- Passive (diastolic) tension curve: rises slowly at first, then steeply, as the ventricle is filled and the relatively inextensible connective-tissue and titin components resist further stretch.
- Active (developed) tension curve: rises with increasing sarcomere length up to an optimal length, because stretch increases myofilament calcium sensitivity and actin-myosin overlap, the basis of the Frank-Starling mechanism; beyond the optimal length, developed tension plateaus and then falls.
- Total tension at any given length is the sum of the passive and active curves.
Unlike skeletal muscle, cardiac muscle normally operates on the ascending limb of this relationship, so increased venous return (preload) almost always increases developed tension and stroke work.

questions.text: Define contractility, and describe its effects on cardiac contraction force.
questions.modelAnswer:
- Cardiac contraction begins when L-type calcium entry during the action potential triggers calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum.
- Calcium binds troponin C, permits actin-myosin cycling, and is then removed by SERCA, the sodium-calcium exchanger, and sarcolemmal calcium pumps.
- Increased preload raises force through the Frank-Starling mechanism, whereas increased afterload reduces shortening and stroke volume.
- Increased contractility raises calcium availability, stroke volume, and ejection fraction while lowering end-systolic volume.

questions.text: What is hypertrophic cardiomyopathy characterized by?
questions.modelAnswer: It is characterized by myocardial hypertrophy (typically asymmetric septal hypertrophy), defective diastolic filling (impaired ventricular relaxation/compliance), and intermittent dynamic left ventricular outflow tract obstruction.
questions.explanation: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is a primarily genetic (sarcomeric protein gene) disease causing disproportionate, often asymmetric septal myocardial hypertrophy without a clear hemodynamic cause. The thickened, stiff myocardium impairs ventricular relaxation, producing defective diastolic filling, while systolic anterior motion of the mitral valve leaflet against the hypertrophied septum can intermittently obstruct the left ventricular outflow tract, especially with exertion or reduced preload.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: The following type of vegetations never gives emboli:
questions.explanation: Rheumatic vegetations are small, sterile, warty deposits of fibrin and platelets firmly attached along the line of valve closure; because they are small and firmly adherent, they essentially never embolize, unlike the bulky, friable vegetations of infective or non-bacterial thrombotic endocarditis. Aschoff bodies and chronic fibrous valve scarring, not embolization, are the characteristic long-term consequence of rheumatic carditis.
questions.keyConcept: Small, firmly adherent rheumatic vegetations rarely embolize

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Vegetations are:
options: Thrombi formed of red blood cells only
Thrombi formed of platelets and fibrin
questions.explanation: Endocardial vegetations are thrombi composed of platelets and fibrin (with variable numbers of trapped inflammatory cells and, in infective endocarditis, colonies of organisms) that form on damaged, abnormal, or infected valve surfaces. They are not pure red-cell clots, are usually friable and detachable (a source of emboli), and are distinct from an ordinary intravascular blood clot in composition and location.
questions.keyConcept: Vegetations are platelet-fibrin thrombi on valve surfaces

questions.explanation: Suppurative pericarditis is bacterial infection of the pericardial space, usually by direct extension from pneumonia or empyema or by hematogenous spread, producing thick fibrinopurulent exudate and carrying a risk of progression to constrictive pericarditis. The correct choice here, “It ends by resolution”, is the statement that matches this principle; the remaining options describe a different structure, value, mechanism, or clinical setting that does not fit what the question asks.
questions.keyConcept: Bacterial pericardial infection with risk of constrictive scarring

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Regarding tuberculous pericarditis:
options: The inflammatory exudate is rich in neutrophils
It can be hemorrhagic, but complete resolution is the usual fate
It is a primary tuberculous infection
questions.explanation: Tuberculous pericarditis results from hematogenous or contiguous spread of Mycobacterium tuberculosis, producing caseous granulomatous inflammation of the pericardium and remaining the most common cause of constrictive pericarditis in endemic regions. The correct choice here, “None of the above”, is the statement that matches this principle; the remaining options describe a different structure, value, mechanism, or clinical setting that does not fit what the question asks.
questions.keyConcept: Caseating granulomatous pericarditis and its constrictive sequela

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: All of the following statements are correct EXCEPT:
options: Spironolactone antagonizes aldosterone receptors decreasing synthesis of a protein that stimulates Na pump
Amiloride acts independent of aldosterone, blocking Na* channel directly
Vasodilator action of thiazides is the basis of their antihypertensive effect
Loop diuretics release PGs which result in vasodilation of efferent arteriole
questions.explanation: Loop-induced prostaglandin vasodilation is mainly at the afferent arteriole. a) Spironolactone antagonizes aldosterone receptors decreasing synthesis of protein that stimulates Na pump - TRUE. b) Amiloride acts independent of aldosterone, blocking Na+ channel - TRUE. c) Vasodilator action of thiazides is basis of antihypertensive effect - TRUE. d) Loop diuretics vasodilate efferent arteriole - FALSE.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Drug of choice in management of edema of liver failure is:
questions.explanation: In liver failure (cirrhosis) edema, spironolactone is drug of choice due to hyperaldosteronism. a) Chlorthalidone - FALSE. b) Spironolactone - TRUE. c) Mannitol - FALSE, contraindicated. d) Acetazolamide - FALSE.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Drug of choice in management of edema of renal failure is:
questions.explanation: In edema of renal failure, loop diuretics such as furosemide are the drugs of choice. a) Chlorthalidone - FALSE, ineffective at low GFR. b) Spironolactone - FALSE, main role is in cirrhosis and as add-on in HF. c) Furosemide - TRUE. d) Acetazolamide - FALSE.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Furosemide is NOT useful for treatment of the following:
questions.explanation: Furosemide is useful in acute pulmonary edema, acute renal failure and hypertensive encephalopathy, but not useful in hypercalciuria as it increases calcium excretion in the urine. a) Acute pulmonary edema - TRUE 25 d b) Acute renal failure - TRUE (for volume overload). c) Hypertensive encephalopathy - TRUE as direct main treatment. d) Hypercalciuria - FALSE, loops increase Ca2+ excretion which aggravate the hyprlercalciuria.
questions.keyConcept: Diuretic classes act at defined nephron sites, producing predictable effects on sodium, water, potassium, acid-base balance, and blood pressure.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Hyponatremia can be aggravated with all the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Hyponatremia is typically aggravated by thiazide and thiazide-like diuretics; loop diuretics less often cause severe hyponatremia because they impair countercurrent concentration. a) Chlorthalidone - TRUE, thiazide-like; can worsen hyponatremia. b) Hydrochlorothiazide - TRUE, classical cause of hyponatremia. c) Furosemide - FALSE, less characteristic than with thiazides. d) Metolazone - TRUE, potent thiazide-like; can aggravate hyponatremia.
questions.keyConcept: Diuretic classes act at defined nephron sites, producing predictable effects on sodium, water, potassium, acid-base balance, and blood pressure.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: In impaired renal function, an effective thiazide like diuretic is:
questions.explanation: is a thiazide-like diuretic effective even in impaired renal function and used with loops in resistant edema. a) Hydrochlorothiazide - FALSE, ineffective at low GFR. b) Chlorthalidone - FALSE at low GFR. c) Metolazone - TRUE. d) Indapamide - FALSE, less effective when GFR is markedly reduced.
questions.keyConcept: Diuretic classes act at defined nephron sites, producing predictable effects on sodium, water, potassium, acid-base balance, and blood pressure.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: In patients with sulfonamide allergy, the following diuretic can be used:
questions.explanation: is a non-sulfonamide loop diuretic suitable in sulfonamide allergy. a) Hydrochlorothiazide - FALSE, sulfonamide. b) Bumetanide - FALSE, sulfonamide loop. c) Acetazolamide - FALSE, sulfonamide CA inhibitor. d) Ethacrynic acid - TRUE. e) Frusemide - FALSE, sulfonamide.
questions.keyConcept: Diuretic classes act at defined nephron sites, producing predictable effects on sodium, water, potassium, acid-base balance, and blood pressure.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: In the management of hypercalcemia, the most useful therapy is:
questions.explanation: In acute hypercalcemia, isotonic saline plus loop diuretics enhance Ca2+ excretion. a) Saline + Spironolactone - FALSE. b) Saline + Mannitol - FALSE for hypercalcemia. c) Saline + Furosemide - TRUE. d) Saline + Hydrochlorothiazide - FALSE, thiazides decrease Ca2+ excretion and worsen hypercalcemia.
questions.keyConcept: Diuretic classes act at defined nephron sites, producing predictable effects on sodium, water, potassium, acid-base balance, and blood pressure.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Indapamide has the following characters EXCEPT:
options: It is used in treatment of hypertension
It is a member of thiazide - like diuretics
It has less metabolic adverse effects than thiazides
Can be given in patient with sulfonamide allergy
questions.explanation: Indapamide is used in treatment of hypertension, is a thiazide-like diuretic, and has less metabolic adverse effects than classical thiazides. a) It is used in treatment of hypertension - TRUE, low-dose indapamide is an antihypertensive. b) It is a member of thiazide - like diuretics - TRUE, it is thiazide-related. c) It has less metabolic adverse effects than thiazides - TRUE, this advantage is highlighted in the text. d) Can be given in patient with sulfonamide allergy - FALSE, it is still a sulfonamide derivative.
questions.keyConcept: Diuretic classes act at defined nephron sites, producing predictable effects on sodium, water, potassium, acid-base balance, and blood pressure.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Loop diuretics are preferred to thiazides in:
options: Fluid overload due to heart failure
Resistant hypertension due to volume expansion
questions.explanation: In fluid overload due to HF and resistant hypertension with volume expansion, loops are preferred; sulfonamide hypersensitivity is not an indication because both loops and thiazides are sulfonamides. a) Fluid overload due to heart failure - TRUE. b) Resistant hypertension due to volume expansion - TRUE. c) Sulfonamide hypersensitivity - FALSE. d) A & B - TRUE. e) All of the above - FALSE.
questions.keyConcept: Diuretic classes act at defined nephron sites, producing predictable effects on sodium, water, potassium, acid-base balance, and blood pressure.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Patients with history of sulfonamide hypersensitivity, suffered head injury with brain edema, which of the following combination is best for him:
questions.explanation: In sulfonamide allergy with brain edema, mannitol (non-sulfonamide osmotic) plus dexamethasone is best; sulfonamide diuretics must be avoided. a) Acetazolamide & mannitol - FALSE, acetazolamide is sulfonamide. b) Metolazone & mannitol - FALSE, metolazone is sulfonamide. c) Dexamethasone & frusemide - FALSE, furosemide is sulfonamide. d) Dexamethasone & mannitol - TRUE.
questions.keyConcept: Diuretic classes act at defined nephron sites, producing predictable effects on sodium, water, potassium, acid-base balance, and blood pressure.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: The following diuretic is NOT secreted through the renal tubules:
questions.explanation: reaches its site from the peritubular circulation and is not secreted into the tubular lumen via organic acid/base transporters like most other diuretics. a) Hydrochlorothiazide - FALSE, thiazides are secreted by organic acid transport in proximal b tubule. b) Spironolactone - TRUE, acts from blood side on aldosterone receptors. c) Frusemide - FALSE, loop diuretics are secreted by organic acid system. d) Triamterene - FALSE, secreted as organic base into distal tubule/collecting duct.
questions.keyConcept: Diuretic classes act at defined nephron sites, producing predictable effects on sodium, water, potassium, acid-base balance, and blood pressure.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: The following diuretics are matched to sheir possible indications EXCEPT:
options: Loop / edema of acute renal failure and acute pulmonary edema
questions.explanation: Hypertensive encephalopathy requires rapid IV antihypertensives (e. g. nitroprusside, IV loop); oral chlorthalidone is not used acutely. a) Mannitol/ Cerebral edema & acute glaucoma - TRUE, classical indication. b) Loop / edema of acute renal failure and acute pulmonary edema - TRUE, loop diuretics are first choice. c) Chlorthalidone/ Hypertensive encephalopathy - FALSE, not appropriate. d) Amiloride / Hypokalemia & hypomagnesemia - TRUE, K+-sparing diuretic used to correct these.
questions.keyConcept: Diuretic classes act at defined nephron sites, producing predictable effects on sodium, water, potassium, acid-base balance, and blood pressure.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: The following is a WRONG statement about pharmacokinetics of loop diuretics:
options: Absorption of furosemide is variable while bumetanide is complete
Elimination of furosemide is renal while of bumetanide is hepatic
Bumetanide requires dose adjustment on switching from oral to intravenous route
questions.explanation: Bumetanide is almost completely absorbed orally and has similar potency IV, so no special dose adjustment is needed when switching routes. a) Absorption of furosemide variable while bumetanide complete - TRUE. b) Elimination of furosemide renal while bumetanide hepatic - TRUE (significant hepatic metabolism). c) Highly bound to plasma protein - TRUE. d) Bumetanide requires dose adjustment oral leads to IV - FALSE.
questions.keyConcept: Diuretic classes act at defined nephron sites, producing predictable effects on sodium, water, potassium, acid-base balance, and blood pressure.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: The following is NOT common between Thiazide & Loop diuretics:
questions.explanation: is characteristic for loop diuretics, not thiazides; hypokalemia, venodilation and hyperuricemia can occur with both. a) Hypokalemia - COMMON to both. b) Ototoxicity - NOT common to both; only loops. c) Venulodilaion - BOTH have some venodilating effect. d) Hyperuricemia - COMMON to both. e) B & C - This option says "NOT common between thiazide & loop diuretics"; since only B is not common, the correct single "NOT common" is b).
questions.keyConcept: Diuretic classes act at defined nephron sites, producing predictable effects on sodium, water, potassium, acid-base balance, and blood pressure.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: The following is NOT expected adverse effect of loop diuretic:
options: Increase risk of thrombosis due to hemoconcentration
questions.explanation: Loop diuretics cause hypocalcemia (increased urinary calcium excretion), not hypercalcemia, so hypercalcemia is the effect that is NOT expected. The other options are genuine, well-documented adverse effects of loop diuretics: cross-hypersensitivity with sulfonamides and myalgia; ototoxicity and interstitial nephritis; increased thrombosis risk from hemoconcentration; and hypokalemia with metabolic alkalosis.
questions.keyConcept: Diuretic classes act at defined nephron sites, producing predictable effects on sodium, water, potassium, acid-base balance, and blood pressure.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: The following is WRONG concerning management of refractoriness to loop diuretics:
options: The diuretic is mixed with albumin and given IV
Triamterene counteracts the decreased Na+ reabsorption seen secondary to hypertrophy of distal tubular cells
Increase furosemide dose up to 5-fold in renal failure
questions.explanation: With chronic loop-diuretic use, distal tubular cells hypertrophy and increase Na+ reabsorption (a cause of diuretic refractoriness); this is countered by adding a thiazide diuretic, not triamterene, so attributing the correction to triamterene is the wrong statement. Mixing the diuretic with albumin and giving it IV is a genuine strategy in hypoalbuminemia, furosemide doses are indeed increased substantially (up to 5-fold) in renal failure, and spironolactone genuinely counteracts aldosterone-dependent Na+ reabsorption, so those statements are correct.
questions.keyConcept: Diuretic classes act at defined nephron sites, producing predictable effects on sodium, water, potassium, acid-base balance, and blood pressure.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following diuretics is matched with its risk in renal impairment:
options: Mannitol / risk of precipitation of acute renal failure
questions.explanation: In acute renal failure or poor filtration, mannitol is not filtered, stays in plasma, expands volume and can precipitate or worsen renal failure, so this risk is real. a) Mannitol / risk of precipitation of acute renal failure - TRUE. b) Chlorthalidone / risk of hyperkalemia - FALSE, thiazides cause hypokalemia. c) Spironolactone / risk of hypokalemia - FALSE, it is potassium-sparing and can cause hyperkalemia. d) Acetazolamide / risk of dehydration - TRUE, due to diuresis and bicarbonate loss. 194 fi Pharmacology
questions.keyConcept: Diuretic classes act at defined nephron sites, producing predictable effects on sodium, water, potassium, acid-base balance, and blood pressure.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following is suitable for refractory edema due to liver failure:
options: Low dose of spironolactone followed by Chlorthalidone
Furosemide followed by Low dose spironolactone
Full dose of spironolactone followed by furosemide
Full dose of frusemide followed by spironolactone
questions.explanation: In refractory edema of liver failure, full-dose spironolactone is started, and if inadequate, loop diuretics like furosemide are added. a) Low dose spironolactone then chlorthalidone - FALSE. b) High dose spironolactone - INCOMPLETE alone. c) Furosemide then low dose spironolactone - WRONG order. d) Full dose spironolactone followed by furosemide - TRUE. e) Full dose frusemide then spironolactone - FALSE.
questions.keyConcept: Diuretic classes act at defined nephron sites, producing predictable effects on sodium, water, potassium, acid-base balance, and blood pressure.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following statement is correct:
options: Loop diuretics are preferred to thiazides in sulfonamide hypersensitivity
Loop diuretics release PGs which result in vasodilation of afferent arterioles
Thiazides inhibit water reabsorption more than sodium reabsorption
Hyponatremia can be aggravated by loop diuretics
questions.explanation: Loops stimulate prostaglandin synthesis causing afferent arteriolar vasodilation and improved GFR. a) Loops preferred to thiazides in sulfonamide hypersensitivity - FALSE, both are sulfonamides 18 except ethacrynic acid. b) Loops release PGs causing afferent vasodilation - TRUE. c) Thiazides inhibit water reabsorption more than sodium - FALSE, they inhibit NaCl reabsorption. d) Hyponatremia can be aggravated by loop diuretics - FALSE; more marked with thiazides.
questions.keyConcept: Diuretic classes act at defined nephron sites, producing predictable effects on sodium, water, potassium, acid-base balance, and blood pressure.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following statements is WRONG:
options: Thiazide diuretics increase toxicity of lithium by increasing its renal reabsorption
NSAIDS increase diuretic effect of loop diuretics
Loop diuretics is used in treatment of hypervolemic dilutional hyponatremia
questions.explanation: NSAIDs inhibit prostaglandin synthesis and thus reduce, not increase, the effect of loop diuretics. a) Thiazides increase lithium toxicity - TRUE, by increasing its reabsorption. b) NSAIDS increase diuretic effect of loop diuretics - FALSE, they decrease it. c) Loop diuretics are used in hypervolemic dilutional hyponatremia - TRUE.
questions.keyConcept: Diuretic classes act at defined nephron sites, producing predictable effects on sodium, water, potassium, acid-base balance, and blood pressure.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: ACEIs have all the following advantages EXCEPT:
options: They induce minimal change in heart rate
They induce no change in potassium level
questions.explanation: ACEIs reduce aldosterone and tend to increase serum K+. a) Minimal change in heart rate - TRUE. b) Preserve renal function - TRUE, especially in diabetics/proteinuric CKD. c) No change in potassium level - FALSE, can cause hyperkalemia. d) Reduce cardiovascular mortality - TRUE.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: All of the following are expected adverse effects of Captopril EXCEPT:
options: Reversible acute renal failure in bilateral renal artery stenosis
Fetotoxic & teratogenic effect if taken during pregnancy
questions.explanation: Captopril, like other ACEIs, tends to cause hyperkalemia, not hypokalemia. a) Reversible acute renal failure in bilateral renal artery stenosis - TRUE, • b) Fetotoxic & teratogenic effect - TRUE, especially 2nd/3rd trimester. c) 1st dose postural hypotension - TRUE. d) Hypokalemia - FALSE, typical is hyperkalemia. e) Dry persistent cough - TRUE, due to bradykinin.
questions.keyConcept: Heart-failure therapy targets congestion, maladaptive neurohormonal activation, afterload, remodeling, and—when appropriate—contractility.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: All of the following drugs increase intracardiac cAMP EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Dopamine, dobutamine increase cAMP via beta-1 receptors, and milrinone increases cAMP by PDE III inhibition; digoxin acts via Na+/K+ ATPase inhibition, not cAMP. a) Dopamine - TRUE. b) Dobutamine - TRUE. c) Milrinone - TRUE. d) Digoxin - FALSE.
questions.keyConcept: Heart-failure therapy targets congestion, maladaptive neurohormonal activation, afterload, remodeling, and—when appropriate—contractility.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Beneficial effects of beta-adrenoceptor blockers in heart failure do NOT include:
options: Resensitize upregulated ß1 receptors in long standing heart failure
questions.explanation: In chronic heart failure, cardiac beta-1 receptors are downregulated by sustained high catecholamine levels. Beta-blockers work by resensitizing and upregulating these downregulated receptors over time, not by “resensitizing upregulated” receptors as the option states, which reverses the actual mechanism and makes it the false, non-beneficial-effect, statement. The other listed effects (decreased heart rate, increased coronary blood flow from a longer diastole, decreased afterload and oxygen demand, and improved left ventricular remodeling) are all genuine, well-documented benefits of beta-blockade in heart failure.
questions.keyConcept: Heart-failure therapy targets congestion, maladaptive neurohormonal activation, afterload, remodeling, and—when appropriate—contractility.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Choose the WRONG statement:
options: Nesiritide is recombinant human type of B-natriuretic peptide
questions.explanation: Milrinone inhibits PDE III and therefore decreases cAMP breakdown, increasing intracellular cAMP. a) Hydralazine is potassium channel opener - TRUE, it causes arteriolar vasodilation via K+ channel d opening. b) Nitroprusside increases intracellular GMP - TRUE, via NO donation. c) Nesiritide is recombinant human type of B-natriuretic peptide - TRUE. d) Milrinone decreases intracellular cAMP - FALSE.
questions.keyConcept: Heart-failure therapy targets congestion, maladaptive neurohormonal activation, afterload, remodeling, and—when appropriate—contractility.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Combination of all the following drugs improve survival time and decrease mortality rate in systolic heart failure EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Loop diuretics improve symptoms and hospitalizations but are not proven to reduce mortality, unlike spironolactone, sacubitril-valsartan and carvedilol. a) Spironolactone - TRUE, mortality +. b) Sacubitril-valsartan - TRUE. c) Furosemide - FALSE as "decrease mortality". d) Carvedilol - TRUE, mortality +. 189 Pharmacology
questions.keyConcept: Heart-failure therapy targets congestion, maladaptive neurohormonal activation, afterload, remodeling, and—when appropriate—contractility.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Frusemide and hydrochlorothiazide have opposite effects on:
questions.explanation: Loop diuretics (furosemide) increase urinary calcium excretion (risk of hypocalcemia), whereas thiazide diuretics (hydrochlorothiazide) decrease urinary calcium excretion (can cause hypercalcemia) by enhancing distal tubular calcium reabsorption, making calcium excretion the parameter on which they have opposite effects. Both classes cause potassium, magnesium, and uric acid excretion in the same (not opposite) direction, so those options are incorrect.
questions.keyConcept: Heart-failure therapy targets congestion, maladaptive neurohormonal activation, afterload, remodeling, and—when appropriate—contractility.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Hypertensive patient with heart failure should NOT be given:
questions.explanation: In HF, non-DHP CCBs such as verapamil are avoided due to negative inotropic effects; thiazides, ACEIs and ARBs are used. a) Thiazides - TRUE, as part of HTN+HF regimens. b) Lisinopril - TRUE, ACEI of choice. c) Valsartan - TRUE, ARB alternative. d) Verapamil - FALSE as "should be given"; it is contraindicated in severe LV dysfunction.
questions.keyConcept: Heart-failure therapy targets congestion, maladaptive neurohormonal activation, afterload, remodeling, and—when appropriate—contractility.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: In congestive heart failure, the following drugs act directly on the myocardium increasing the cardiac output EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: improves CO indirectly by reducing afterload; digoxin, dopamine and dobutamine act directly on myocardium as positive inotropes. a) Captopril - FALSE as "direct inotrope"; effect is indirect. b) Digoxin - TRUE, direct inotrope. c) Dopamine - TRUE at ß doses. d) Dobutamine - TRUE.
questions.keyConcept: Heart-failure therapy targets congestion, maladaptive neurohormonal activation, afterload, remodeling, and—when appropriate—contractility.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Management of digoxin bradyarrhythmia includes:

questions.keyConcept: Heart-failure therapy targets congestion, maladaptive neurohormonal activation, afterload, remodeling, and—when appropriate—contractility.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Manifestations of digoxin toxicity include all the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Digoxin toxicity causes GI upset, CNS symptoms, visual disturbances and arrhythmias rather than isolated severe hypotension. a) Mental confusion - TRUE. b) Visual disturbances - TRUE. c) Severe hypotension - FALSE. d) Vomiting - TRUE.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: The following are contraindication for ACEIs & ARBS EXCEPT:

Chronic kidney disease with preserved kidney function

questions.keyConcept: Heart-failure therapy targets congestion, maladaptive neurohormonal activation, afterload, remodeling, and—when appropriate—contractility.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: The following drug did NOT approve to decrease mortality rate in systolic heart failure:

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: The following drug should be avoided in treatment of digoxin toxicity:
questions.explanation: interacts with digoxin, increasing its level and toxicity, so it should be avoided in digoxin toxicity; the others are used in management. a) Atropine - TRUE, used in digoxin-induced bradycardia/AV block. b) Potassium chloride - TRUE, if K+ <3.5 mmol/L and no AV block. c) Lidocaine - TRUE, for ventricular arrhythmias. d) Digi-bind - TRUE, specific antidote. e) Amiodarone - FALSE as "should be used"; it worsens toxicity.

questions.subject: Pharmacology

questions.subject: Pharmacology

questions.subject: Pharmacology

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: The following is used in treatment of digoxin induced ventricular tachycardia (digoxin toxicity):

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Valsartan has the following advantages over lisinopril EXCEPT:

No hormonal "escape" seen with prolonged ACEIs therapy

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following is a WRONG statement regarding digoxin:

questions.text: Compare continuous, fenestrated, and sinusoidal capillaries by structure and site.
questions.modelAnswer:
- Continuous capillaries have uninterrupted endothelium and basal lamina and occur in muscle, connective tissue, lung, and the central nervous system.
- Fenestrated capillaries have endothelial pores, usually with diaphragms, plus a continuous basal lamina and occur in endocrine glands, intestinal mucosa, and kidney; adult glomerular fenestrae lack diaphragms.
- Sinusoids have a wide irregular lumen, discontinuous endothelium, and discontinuous or absent basal lamina and occur in liver, spleen, and bone marrow.
